findings.claim: Darwin’s On the Origin of Species (1859) had suggested that humans evolved from animals
findings.truth: On the Origin of Species set out evolution by natural selection but did not present a human-evolution argument; Darwin addressed human evolution directly in The Descent of Man (1871).
findings.evidence: Primary text context; Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859) and The Descent of Man (1871).

findings.claim: 40 marks — Shakespeare Essay
findings.truth: This is the 19th-century prose question, not Shakespeare. Only extract-based tasks should be presented as the 40-mark exam format; discursive prompts are useful only as untimed whole-text practice.
findings.evidence: Specification sections 2a and 3a; supplied board facts for Component 01 Section B.

findings.claim: Bye Street
findings.truth: The text calls the location a ‘by-street’; it is not a proper name.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 1, lines 195 and 245; ch. 2, line 813.

findings.claim: ‘small man’; ‘a look so ugly it brought out the sweat on me like running’; Carew’s ‘silvery hair’; ‘trampled’ in the Carew scene
findings.truth: Enfield says ‘little man’ and that Hyde ‘gave me one look, so ugly that it brought out the sweat on me like running’. Carew has ‘white hair’, and Hyde is ‘trampling’ him after clubbing him to the earth.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 1, lines 281–303; ch. 4, lines 1383 and 1421–1427.

findings.claim: The novella’s first moment of clear violence comes with Sir Danvers Carew’s murder.
findings.truth: Hyde’s trampling of the child in Chapter 1 is already a clear act of violence; Carew’s murder is an escalation.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 1, lines 281–303; ch. 4, lines 1413–1427.

findings.claim: Enfield tells Utterson, who reads the will, who hears Poole, who hears the maid.
findings.truth: An anonymous third-person narrator follows Utterson. Enfield’s account and the maid’s report are embedded accounts; Poole does not hear the maid’s report.
findings.evidence: Primary text chs. 1–4, especially ch. 4 line 1483, where the inspector narrates what the maid saw.

findings.claim: a small red shilling edition
findings.truth: The first edition was a paper-covered volume costing one shilling; ‘red’ is unsupported.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg, The Works of Robert Louis Stevenson, Swanston Edition, vol. I, publication account.

findings.claim: 40 marks — Shakespeare Essay
findings.truth: The extract-led items are 19th-century novel questions; the two discursive items are untimed whole-text practice, not the 40-mark exam format.
findings.evidence: Specification sections 2a and 3a; supplied board facts.

findings.claim: Mr Guest ... declares it a forgery
findings.truth: Guest observes that the two hands are largely identical but differently sloped. Utterson privately concludes that Jekyll forged the letter.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 5, lines 1975–2043.

findings.claim: ‘a death warrant written legibly upon his face… he had his death-warrant written there’
findings.truth: The exact line is ‘He had his death-warrant written legibly upon his face.’
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 6, line 2125.

findings.claim: Lanyon is ‘hide-bound’, sticking to ‘the practical side of medicine’.
findings.truth: Jekyll calls Lanyon a ‘hide-bound pedant’; ‘the practical side of medicine’ is not in the text.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 3, lines 1227–1233; no occurrence of ‘practical side’ in the primary text.

findings.claim: early Freud ... questioning the unity of the self [in the 1880s]
findings.truth: Freud’s psychoanalytic model belongs mainly to the 1890s and later. William James is an appropriate contemporary reference for 1880s debates about consciousness.
findings.evidence: Publication chronology: William James’s psychology work appeared through the 1870s–1880s; Freud’s psychoanalytic work developed in the 1890s.

findings.claim: the hand glimpsed on the stair is ‘dwarfish’ and ‘hairy’, and a servant girl saw a creature ‘crying out like a rat’
findings.truth: Poole cites the altered voice, the figure’s dwarfish build and its light, odd footsteps. No servant girl reports a hairy hand or a creature crying like a rat.

findings.claim: two documents ... the reader ... does not yet know why Jekyll’s body is Hyde’s
findings.truth: Several enclosures fall from Jekyll’s envelope, including the revised will, a note and his confession. The body is Hyde’s; Jekyll has disappeared.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 8, lines 3161–3175 and 3315–3387.

findings.claim: ‘The letter is a forgery,’ said the lawyer, ‘the man has forged it.’ / 40 marks — Shakespeare Essay
findings.truth: That quotation is invented. Guest comments on the resemblance between the hands. The labels must distinguish the 19th-century novel format from untimed discursive practice.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 5, lines 2009–2043; specification sections 2a and 3a.

findings.claim: a drug that ‘could cast off the lower elements’ of his personality
findings.truth: This is not a quotation. Jekyll says the drug dethroned existing powers and substituted a form bearing the stamp of lower elements in his soul.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 10, lines 4101–4137.

findings.claim: wakes in a park one morning as Hyde without taking it
findings.truth: After the Carew murder, Jekyll transforms while awake on a bench in Regent’s Park. The earlier involuntary awakening as Hyde happens in his own bed before the murder.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 10, lines 4459–4575 and 4805–4835.

findings.claim: Stevenson himself called the book ‘a fable’
findings.truth: No reliable Stevenson attribution was found for this wording. His 1886 letter to John Addington Symonds instead calls its subject ‘the war in the members’.
findings.evidence: Project Gutenberg, The Letters of Robert Louis Stevenson, vol. XXIV, letter to John Addington Symonds, 1886.

findings.claim: 40 marks — Shakespeare Essay
findings.truth: The extract-led items are 19th-century novel questions; the discursive items are untimed whole-text practice.
findings.evidence: Specification sections 2a and 3a; supplied board facts.

findings.claim: Utterson is ... the novella’s primary narrator / ‘lean, cold, scanty, and yet somehow lovable’
findings.truth: An anonymous third-person narrator follows Utterson for most of the first eight chapters. The exact compact description is ‘lean, long, dusty, dreary and yet somehow lovable’.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 1, lines 119–125; narrative form of chs. 1–8.

findings.claim: 40 marks — Shakespeare Essay
findings.truth: Quotation-led items can be used for 19th-century novel practice; discursive prompts must not be presented as the 40-mark exam format.
findings.evidence: Specification sections 2a and 3a; supplied board facts.

findings.claim: The front faces a respectable square: ‘a certain sinister block of building’ with ‘a great air of wealth and comfort.’
findings.truth: The front door in the square wears ‘a great air of wealth and comfort’. The ‘sinister block of building’ is the neglected rear seen from the by-street.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 1, lines 219–233; ch. 2, lines 1023–1037.

findings.claim: a ‘dismal’ former dissecting theatre
findings.truth: The laboratory block is ‘dingy’ and ‘windowless’; the theatre is ‘gaunt and silent’. ‘Dismal’ describes Soho and a screech, not the laboratory.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 5, lines 1687–1707; occurrences of ‘dismal’ at lines 1531 and 3129.

findings.claim: How many narrators does the novella have? Correct answer: Three / Utterson, Dr Lanyon, and Jekyll
findings.truth: Utterson is a focal character, not the narrator. A safer account is three main narrative stages: anonymous third-person narration focused on Utterson, Lanyon’s first-person narrative and Jekyll’s first-person statement.
findings.evidence: Primary text narrative form across chs. 1–10.

findings.claim: 40 marks — Shakespeare Essay
findings.truth: Quotation-led items can be used for 19th-century novel practice; discursive prompts must be labelled as untimed whole-text practice.
findings.evidence: Specification sections 2a and 3a; supplied board facts.

findings.claim: Enfield hides what he saw
findings.truth: Enfield tells Utterson what he saw, then agrees with him not to refer to the matter again.
findings.evidence: Primary text ch. 1, lines 243–557.

findings.claim: may offer a choice between an extract-based task and a discursive task, both assessing AO1, AO2 and AO3 / What are the three assessment objectives tested in Section B?
findings.truth: Students choose one of two 40-mark extract-based questions. It is closed book, and this section also assesses accurate spelling, punctuation, grammar, vocabulary and sentence structure. The specification gives no per-question numerical AO split.
findings.evidence: Specification sections 2a, 3a, 3b and 3h; supplied board facts.

findings.claim: 40 marks — Shakespeare Essay
findings.truth: The quotation-led item can be used for 19th-century novel practice; the discursive prompts are untimed whole-text practice rather than the exam format.
findings.evidence: Specification sections 2a and 3a; supplied board facts.

summary: Checked all seven lessons against the specification and primary text. The main risks were a systemic Shakespeare/exam-format mislabelling, omission of SPaG, invented or conflated quotations, and incorrect narration or plot claims.
